name: Craniosacral therapy

lead: Craniosacral therapy (CST) is an alternative manual therapy in which a practitioner uses light touch on the head, spine and sacrum to detect and adjust a rhythm said to travel through the cerebrospinal fluid. A few looksmaxxing posters try it hoping to adjust skull bones, bite and posture for better facial symmetry.

It grew out of cranial osteopathy by William Sutherland and was developed by John Upledger. Proponents hold that skull bones move in a cycle at roughly 6 to 12 cycles per minute and that therapists can feel and release restrictions. Studies have found practitioners cannot reliably identify the rhythm, systematic reviews report limited evidence, and medical reviews describe the premise as inconsistent with anatomy.

paras: Clients lie clothed on a table while the practitioner holds the head, neck and lower back with light pressure, typically over a series of sessions of 30 to 60 minutes.

Reviews describe manipulation of the skull as potentially harmful, particularly for infants and children, and report at least two deaths linked to CST spinal manipulation as of 2018. The American Cancer Society advises against use on children under two, and using it as the only treatment for serious illness has been cautioned against.

chain: Light touch to skull and spine
angle.text: Some users try craniosacral therapy hoping that light touch on the skull and spine will adjust skull bones and improve facial symmetry. The therapy rests on a claimed cranial rhythm, and reviews report limited evidence of benefit.

lead: Craniosacral therapy (CST) is a form of alternative medicine in which practitioners use light touch to feel purported rhythmic movements of the skull bones and spine and to adjust them. It grew out of cranial osteopathy devised by William Garner Sutherland in the early twentieth century, and was developed by osteopath John Upledger, who ran research on the purported pulse at Michigan State University between 1975 and 1983 [1][2].

Practitioners claim it treats conditions such as chronic pain, headaches, fibromyalgia and anxiety [2]. Systematic reviews report limited and methodologically weak evidence, and medical reviews describe the premise as inconsistent with skull, brain and spine anatomy and physiology [1][2].
In looksmaxxing communities it appears in discussions of cranial movement, bite and posture, usually as a theory rather than a procedure with studied appearance outcomes.
infobox: Unregulated in the UK per Ernst (2005 listing)

paras: CST holds that cerebrospinal fluid, meninges and cranial bones form a semi-closed hydraulic system that produces a palpable rhythm, which therapists assess and try to correct with gentle touch and techniques such as a so-called still point [2]. Sutherland noted that skull sutures are bevelled and proposed that they remain mobile, an idea he called the primary respiratory mechanism [1][2]. Upledger's later formulation added the idea of somatoemotional release, in which physical restrictions are said to hold unresolved emotion [2].

A 2011 review found the evidence sparse and too heterogeneous for conclusions, and a 2012 systematic review by Edzard Ernst found that claims beyond non-specific effects lack support from rigorous randomised trials [1]. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials for chronic pain reported limited evidence of pain relief for up to six months [3], a finding that McGill University's Office for Science and Society disputed because the underlying studies were methodologically weak [1].

Tests of practitioners have found they cannot reliably detect the craniosacral pulse, and different practitioners reach different results for the same patient [1][2]. A review of manual therapies for tension-type headache also looked at this field's evidence [4]. The American Cancer Society states that available evidence does not support claims that CST helps treat cancer or any other disease [1].

Reviews describe skull manipulation as potentially harmful, particularly for infants and children, and the American Cancer Society advises against use on children under two [1]. As of 2018 at least two deaths had been linked to CST spinal manipulation, and a small study found people with head injuries worsened after treatment [1]. A literature review has examined adverse events from chiropractic and other manual therapies in infants and children [5].

Randomised trials of CST have studied chronic pain conditions, not appearance. A trial in fibromyalgia patients examined effects on pain and heart rate variability [6], and a 2019 meta-analysis pooled randomised trials for chronic pain [3]. No studies have examined CST for facial or skull shape.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, craniosacral rhythm appears in a theory thread about skull flexion and extension, occlusion and posture, and drew sceptical replies.

claims.claim: The skull flexes and extends in a craniosacral rhythm driven by the sphenoid and occipital bones

Upledger and Retzlaff run research on the purported cranial pulse at Michigan State University [1].
